paper.abstract_en: A negative muon captured by an actinide cascades down through the muonic atomic levels; deeply bound transitions can proceed via inverse internal conversion, depositing the muonic transition energy directly into the nucleus and, when the deposited energy exceeds the fission barrier, inducing prompt fission. Because the muon mean lifetime exceeds the saddle-to-scission timescale by orders of magnitude, the muon can survive the entire fission event as a <math><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> spectator and ultimately attach to one or both of the emerging fragments. Its postscission attachment probability to the light fragment, <math><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></math>, can be used as a direct electromagnetic probe of fission dynamics on a timescale of <math><mrow><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>21</mn></mrow></msup><mspace width="0.28em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow></math>. In previous work, we introduced a three-dimensional lattice solution of the time-dependent Dirac equation coupled to the electromagnetic field generated by a fissioning nucleus and reported <math><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></math> for several actinides at a single dissipation strength. Here we extend that framework to a systematic survey of <math><mmultiscripts><mi>Th</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>232</mn></mmultiscripts><mo>,</mo><mo> </mo><mmultiscripts><mi mathvariant="normal">U</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>238</mn></mmultiscripts></math>, and <math><mmultiscripts><mi>Pu</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mn>240</mn></mmultiscripts></math> and implement a more realistic fission model which incorporates dynamic pairing correlations. We find that <math><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></math> falls steeply with the fragment charge asymmetry, a robust structural fingerprint of the fissioning system, while its dependence on nuclear dissipation is secondary and sensitive to the phenomenological friction prescription. These results establish <math><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></math> as a clean electromagnetic probe of fragment charge asymmetry and motivate a self-consistent, coordinate- and time-dependent treatment of nuclear dissipation as the natural next step.
